name: Bianca Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Hollow Lane, a pig unit with about six hundred sows, and the family grows wheat and barley on three hundred hectares to feed them. I'm on the farrowing side, where the sows have their piglets. I'm in at six, check every pen, clean out, make sure no piglet's been lain on in the night, and by ten my back knows about it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and what came before?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Three years. Before that I raised four children and kept house, and I ran the church kitchen on Sundays and for every funeral in the parish. Then my husband Dieter's hours were cut at the sawmill, and we needed money, so I asked old Mr Harding at Hollow Lane, who's in our congregation. He gave me a chance, and I've tried to repay it by never missing a day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what's hard about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the little ones. A newborn piglet that's cold, you rub it with straw and put it under the lamp, and ten minutes later it's fighting its brothers for a teat. What's hard is that I'm slow and I'm still learning. The young manager, Kyle, writes everything on a tablet and gets impatient when I ask him to say it out loud. And money's tight, we've got about two weeks put by, and the house needs a roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, keep it in its place. A tool is a tool. I'd say it after church, where people would nod, because most of them are like me and don't trust that sort of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I don't think about it much. I've never used one of those AI things, I wouldn't know how to start, and I don't want to. If it stays as a better search engine, it's Kyle's business, not mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do what I do now. Work my shifts, pray, help at the kitchen, keep the money tight. Maybe I'd let Kyle show me the tablet properly, but only because he's tired of me asking him to read things out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The pigs don't read the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't want to use AI. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen what screens do to people. My grandchildren sit at the dinner table with their heads down like they're praying, and they're not. I'd rather learn the pigs from the pigs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has Kyle's tablet ever caused you trouble?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter it said a sow was due on the Thursday, and she farrowed on the Tuesday night. I'd said she was close, because she was making her nest, tearing at the straw. Kyle believed the tablet. We lost two piglets.

S0.say: I'd say keep it in its place, a tool is a tool. I'd say it after church, where most people would agree.
S0.think: I don't think about it much. I've never used AI and don't want to, and if it stays a search engine it's the young manager's business, not mine.
S0.do: Carries on with her shifts, church kitchen and tight budget. Lets the young manager show her the tablet properly, mainly because he's tired of reading things out to her.
S0.feel: Calm. As she puts it, the pigs don't read the news.
S0.quote: My grandchildren sit at the dinner table with their heads down like they're praying, and they're not.
S0.fieldNote: Bianca's distrust of screens is moral as much as practical, and her church life is central. The story of the tablet getting a farrowing date wrong showed she has her own kind of expertise, built on watching animals. She's proud of never missing a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second one. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's how it should be, slow and careful, and businesses have every right to run as they see fit. But I'd say it's a shame if young people don't get a start, because a job teaches you more than school ever did. Apprenticeships, that's what I'd want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one doesn't trouble me much for myself. Slow suits me. What I'd mind is my grandsons, Lukas and Ben, who are seventeen and fifteen and not much for books. If nobody takes beginners, what do boys like that do?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Harding, after church, whether he'd take Lukas on for weekends. I'd work a bit harder so he can see what a Wagner is worth. And I'd tell Lukas to get off his phone and get his hands dirty, which he'd ignore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for the boys. Calm for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask Mr Harding after church rather than at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because at work he's the boss and I'm the help. After church, we're neighbours. Things get done between neighbours that don't get done across a desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if Lukas said no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him his great-grandfather started at fourteen mucking out, and nobody asked him if he felt like it. Then I'd make him a bacon sandwich, because shouting doesn't work on that boy.

S1.say: I'd say slow and careful is right and businesses can run as they see fit. But it's a shame if young people don't get a start, and I'd want apprenticeships.
S1.think: This one doesn't trouble me much for myself, because slow suits me. I'd mind for my grandsons, who aren't much for books.
S1.do: Asks the farm owner after church whether he'd take her older grandson on for weekends. Works harder to prove the family's worth and tells the boy to get off his phone.
S1.feel: Uneasy for her grandsons, calm for herself.
S1.quote: Things get done between neighbours that don't get done across a desk.
S1.fieldNote: Her traditional outlook showed in trusting businesses to decide while wanting apprenticeships. She works through church and neighbourly ties, not formal channels. Her worry was for grandsons who aren't academic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should stand on their own two feet, and families should look after each other, not wait for the government. Politicians shouting won't fix anything. I'd say it at the kitchen to the other women, and some would agree and some would go quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my daughter Annika works in the office at the building society in town, and that's exactly the job you're describing. I'd be worried sick. And I don't really know what I'd tell her, because standing on your own feet is easier to say when your own feet aren't the ones being kicked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Annika she and the children can always come to us, we'd squeeze in. I'd ask the church to start a little job board, people helping each other find work, the way we do with meals when someone's poorly. And I'd stop the bit I put by for the roof and keep it for whoever needs it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a heavy feeling about Annika. I'd pray about it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said standing on your own feet is easier when your feet aren't being kicked. That sounds like a change of mind.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's not a change, it's a worry. I still believe it. I just know it's harder for someone with three children and a mortgage. Both things are true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the church job board look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A cork board at the back of the hall, and Pastor Brenner reading it out at the end of the service. Someone needs a hand with their garden, someone's son needs work, someone knows a firm that's hiring. That's how it was when I was a girl, before everything went on screens.

S2.say: I'd say people should stand on their own feet and families should look after each other instead of waiting for government. Politicians shouting won't fix it.
S2.think: My daughter works in a building society office, exactly the job described, and I'd be worried sick. Standing on your own feet is easier to say when yours aren't the ones being kicked.
S2.do: Tells her daughter the family can move in if needed. Asks the church to start a job board so members help each other find work, and holds the roof money for whoever needs it first.
S2.feel: Uneasy and heavy about her daughter. She'd pray about it.
S2.quote: Standing on your own feet is easier to say when your own feet aren't the ones being kicked.
S2.fieldNote: The office picture tested her self-reliance views against her daughter's situation, and she held both. Her answer was family and church, not government: a cork board at the back of the hall. When I named the tension, she said both things were true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains belong to the people who built the businesses, but they ought to show some decency and look after their own workers. And I'd say it's not the government's job to take it all and hand it out. Families and churches and employers who care, that's how it should work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be grateful I've got my hands in muck. Pigs need feeding whatever the stock market does. But Dieter's at the sawmill, and they build houses with that timber, so with a house boom maybe his hours come back. That would be a mercy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Dieter to go to the sawmill manager and ask for full hours back, straight away, before anyone else does. If he got them, the first money goes on the roof. I'd keep doing my shifts and put in for the extra Saturday cleaning at the unit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for the country and for Annika, but a bit hopeful at home. I'm not used to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for the political crisis in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People who never did a day's work with their hands, on both sides, shouting about money they didn't earn. And maybe the big computer companies, for rushing. I don't trust anyone who moves that fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said decency rather than government. What if the employers don't show any?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then people should take their custom elsewhere, and God will judge the rest. I know that's not much of an answer for someone who's lost their job. It's the one I've got.

S3.say: I'd say the gains belong to those who built the businesses, but they should show decency to their own workers. It's not government's job to take it all and hand it out.
S3.think: I'd be grateful my hands are in muck, since pigs need feeding whatever the markets do. A house boom might even bring my husband's sawmill hours back.
S3.do: Gets her husband to ask the sawmill manager for full hours back right away and earmarks the first extra money for the roof. Takes extra Saturday cleaning at the pig unit.
S3.feel: Uneasy for the country and her daughter, but unusually hopeful at home.
S3.quote: Then people should take their custom elsewhere, and God will judge the rest. I know that's not much of an answer for someone who's lost their job.
S3.fieldNote: Her free-market and faith views shaped who she blamed: people who don't work with their hands, and companies that rush. She admitted her answer of decency and divine judgement is thin comfort to someone laid off. A house boom could actually help her husband's sawmill work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong to throw loyal people out for a machine, and that a business that does it will answer for it, one way or another. I wouldn't ask the government to ban robots, that's not right either. But I'd say it plainly, at church and at the farm, that loyalty should count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Mr Harding would keep me as long as he could, because I'm in his congregation and he's a decent man. But he's seventy-four, and his son Martin runs the numbers, and Martin is a tablet man like Kyle. I'd be gone within the year, and I wouldn't blame Martin, which is the worst of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work every hour I was given right to the end, so nobody could say I slacked. I'd ask the church job board for anything, cleaning, cooking, care work, though you say robots are in care homes too. We'd stop the car insurance on the old car and sell it, and if it came to it, Dieter and I would move in with our son Stefan, who's a welder and has a spare room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I keep thinking of those piglets under the lamp, and that I'd not be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandchildren?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That their grandmother worked till the last day and wasn't ashamed. And that they should learn to do something with their hands that a machine can't, though I wouldn't know what to tell them that is anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever learn to work with the robots, if that was the only job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think I could. I can barely read Kyle's tablet. I'm not too proud, I'd try, but I know myself, and they'd be better off with a young person.

S4.say: I'd say it's wrong to throw loyal people out for a machine, and such a business will answer for it. I wouldn't ask for a ban, but I'd say plainly that loyalty should count.
S4.think: The owner would keep me as long as he could, but his son runs the numbers and likes tablets. I'd be gone within the year, and I wouldn't even blame him.
S4.do: Works every hour to the end so nobody can call her a slacker and asks the church job board for any work. Sells the old car and, if needed, moves in with her welder son.
S4.feel: Alarmed, thinking of the piglets under the lamp and that she wouldn't be there.
S4.quote: I'd be gone within the year, and I wouldn't blame Martin, which is the worst of it.
S4.fieldNote: She stayed true to her views: no ban, but a moral case for loyalty. She was resigned to losing the job and, painfully, wouldn't blame the farmer's son for it. Her plan rested on family and church, and she doubted she could learn to work with robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The last one. The others happen to other people, and I can help them. That one happens to me, and to the grandchildren after me. What would help is employers who keep their older people on, even part-time, and proper apprenticeships for the young ones. And I'd like the church to be the place people turn to first, like it used to be.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. I know it's not your business. But a lot of people like me will get through whatever comes because they've got a congregation around them, and the ones who haven't will have it much harder.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Thank you. Is there anything else?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'd like someone to ask the sows what they think of a robot. I'm half joking. But only half.

headlineQuote: I'd be gone within the year, and I wouldn't blame Martin, which is the worst of it.
portrait: Bianca Wagner is 58 and has spent three years on the farrowing side of a 600-sow pig and arable unit, after raising four children and running her church kitchen. She took the job when her husband Dieter's sawmill hours were cut, has about two weeks of savings, never uses AI, and trusts what she sees in the animals over the manager's tablet. Her faith and belief in self-reliance shape every answer: she looks to family, church and decent employers, not government, though she admits that standing on your own feet is harder when your daughter's office job is at risk. In the robot picture she is alarmed and resigned, expecting to be let go by the owner's son and refusing to blame him.
biggestWorry: The robot picture worries her most, because it hits her own job and her grandchildren's future.
whatWouldHelp: Employers who keep older workers on, even part-time, and proper apprenticeships for young people, with the church as a first place to turn.
